title: The Curse Of Good Intentions
gist: Gavekal argues the Reserve Bank of India's administrative curbs on currency hedging to defend the rupee may backfire by deterring the foreign inflows needed to ease depreciation, after a summer expat-dollar scheme (US$130bn) briefly seemed to have stabilized the currency. Teaser only; the full argument is paywalled.

insights.claim: The Reserve Bank of India's administrative curbs on currency hedging risk deterring the very foreign capital inflows India needs to ease rupee depreciation pressure.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Foreign investors facing hedging restrictions may cut India exposure, adding to rupee weakness rather than relieving it; watch FPI flows after the curbs.
insights.quote: By imposing administrative curbs on currency hedging, the central bank may deter the very foreign capital inflows needed to ease depreciation pressures.
insights.locator: The Reserve Bank of India’s increasingly heavy-handed efforts

insights.claim: Gavekal frames the RBI's increasingly heavy-handed rupee defence through Lant Pritchett's 'flailing state' lens: limited Indian state capacity frustrates even well-intentioned policies.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Treat Indian policy interventions in markets as carrying execution risk; well-meant measures can create unintended capital-flow distortions.
insights.quote: dubbed India a “flailing state” where limited state capacity often frustrates even well-intentioned policies
insights.locator: It is the sort of policy predicament

insights.claim: The Indian rupee has fallen 5.5% against the US dollar in 2026, making it one of Asia's weakest currencies, after sliding since mid-2025.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: INR underperformance versus Asian peers signals sustained external-balance stress for India.
insights.locator: The Indian rupee has been sliding since mid-2025

insights.claim: The rupee's decline accelerated after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz in March 2026 sent oil prices soaring, with higher fuel prices, foreign capital outflows and rising global interest rates all pressuring the currency.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: India's oil-import dependence makes INR a short-oil proxy; Hormuz disruption and higher global rates are key rupee risk factors.
insights.locator: The Indian rupee has been sliding since mid-2025

insights.claim: An RBI special scheme launched in early June 2026 to attract US dollars from wealthy expatriate Indians generated about US$130bn of inflows over the summer.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Diaspora deposit schemes can deliver large one-off FX buffers, but they are a temporary fix rather than a structural inflow.
insights.locator: To stem the sell-off, the RBI launched a special scheme

insights.claim: The US$130bn expat inflow comfortably exceeded India's expected 2026 current account deficit of about US$80bn plus equity portfolio outflows of about US$30bn, so the worst seemed over for the rupee, a view Gavekal implies has since been undermined.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The apparent financing cushion did not end rupee pressure, suggesting the RBI's subsequent hedging curbs reflect renewed stress; be wary of calling a bottom in INR.
insights.quote: it seemed the worst was over for the currency
insights.locator: Against an expected current account deficit
